title: Intersectional genetics: the AND-gate
objective: Explain how requiring Cre AND Flp restricts expression to one population, and how the colon paper used it to exclude non-DRG neurons.

steps.title: The problem one marker can't solve
steps.body: A marker like *Calca* (CGRP) is expressed in the [[DRG]] neurons you want — **and** in enteric, sympathetic, or nodose neurons you don't. One [[Cre]] line alone can't separate them. You need a second criterion.

steps.title: Require two features at once
steps.body: Use a payload that needs **both** Cre and [[Flp]]. Drive **Cre** from one feature (your molecular marker) and **Flp** from another (e.g. a gene expressed in DRG but not the unwanted populations). Only cells that are **both** — marker-positive AND DRG — light up. It's a Venn-diagram intersection instead of a single hunt for the perfect gene.

visual.alt: Three neurons: Cre-only and Flp-only stay off; only the neuron with both Cre and Flp switches the payload on.
visual.caption: AND-gate: only the Cre + Flp neuron expresses the payload.

steps.prompt: Marker X is in your DRG neurons but also in nearby sympathetic neurons. You add a Flp driver active in DRG but not sympathetic neurons, and a Cre+Flp-dependent payload. What expresses the payload?
options: Every marker-X cell, in both DRG and sympathetic neurons
Only marker-X cells that are also DRG (Cre AND Flp present)
Only the sympathetic neurons, since Flp overrides Cre there
No cells at all, because the two drivers cancel each other
steps.explanation: The AND-gate keeps only the overlap: marker-positive AND DRG. The sympathetic cells have Cre but not Flp, so they stay off.

variants.setup: Marker X is in your DRG neurons and in nearby sympathetic neurons. You add a Flp driver on in DRG but off in sympathetic, with a Cre+Flp payload.
options: Every marker-X cell, in both DRG and sympathetic neurons
Only marker-X cells that are also DRG (Cre AND Flp present)
Only the sympathetic neurons, since Flp overrides Cre there
No cells at all, because the two drivers cancel each other
variants.reveal: The intersection keeps only cells with both drivers — marker-X AND DRG — excluding the sympathetic cells.

steps.scenario: Your single Cre line (a broad sensory marker) labels DRG neurons but also enteric neurons in the gut wall, confounding a colon experiment.
options: Give less tamoxifen so fewer enteric neurons get labeled
Add a Flp driver on in DRG, off in enteric, with a Cre+Flp payload
Switch to a brighter reporter so DRG cells stand out more
Change the payload from GFP to tdTomato for better contrast
steps.explanation: This is exactly the colon paper's strategy: [[intersectional genetics|intersectional]] (and subtractive) genetics to isolate DRG afferents from enteric, sympathetic, and nodose neurons that share markers. Dose and [[reporter]] color don't fix a specificity problem.
steps.followUp: Retrograde viral labeling from the organ (C4) can add anatomical specificity on top of genetic specificity.

steps.title: Why this is the lab's default move
steps.body: Almost every specificity question gets answered by **composing features** rather than finding one magic marker. Markers are leaky; intersections are sharp. When you read a Wolfson/Ginty methods section, expect Cre + Flp combinations doing this work.

flag.note: Exact driver/allele combinations are in each paper's methods — check there before quoting specific lines.
